doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Juggling educator, scorer and player; scoring pays best per hour
summary: Berg describes his many hats; he sees himself as a jazz pianist, but scoring commercials and orchestrating for rock stars pays the most per hour.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Yeah, my life is about hats. Yeah. Educator, doing a fair bit of composing and scoring and traveling around and playing, and so yeah, it’s a juggling act.
Do you favor one over the other?

It’s an interesting thing. I think when I look at myself in the mirror in the morning I see a jazz piano player. I think that that’s how I define myself. But if you think of the playing, the teaching and the scoring maybe being the order of fulfillment, if you flip it upside down that’s the pay scale. So it’s just one of those interesting things about life.
What’s on the top of the pay scale?
The scoring job, in terms of the money per hours.

For instance if you’re doing a network 30-second spot for a commercial, it may take you two hours to score the whole thing, and yet the pay can be a lot. Or working doing an orchestration for a rock star or something like that, per hour, that’s probably the highest in terms of pay of the things that I do.
Great. We’ll have to talk more about that. At what point in your young life I guess, did it seem like music was going to be your thing?
